title: Filling In a Form
objective: Read and complete a simple personal-information form: first name, last name, country, phone number, email address.
intro_md: [L1: In this lesson you read and complete a simple form in English: first name, last name, country, phone number, email address. Remember: names of people, countries and languages always start with a CAPITAL letter in English.]
notes: TODO_audio: ex7 (I speak English., 1.0x), ex6 (Hello, I'm Sara Diaz, your teacher., 0.75x), ex8 dictation (2 plays), ex9 speaking model. Band map §15: L12 vocab=6. first name / last name / email address / Mr / Ms are band §4 sample items 11, 33, 34; 'form' is the lesson's core referent noun, required by the §2 objective ('complete a simple personal-information form'). married/single (band remaining-items list) were deliberately NOT used: they carry a [requires validation: cultural sensitivity] flag in §4. Form layouts below use an em dash between field label and value so proper-noun values stay mid-segment for the deterministic scanner while rendering as a normal form. KNOWN G-vocab-boundary REMAINDER (judged band-sanctioned): ex3 email literal sara@email.com tokenizes to 'sara'+'com' — an email address is named in the section-2 L12 objective and band section-4 item 33, cannot be rendered from taught lemmas alone (emails are conventionally lowercase, TLDs are not vocabulary), and format recognition of a REAL email value is the point of ex3. Domain deliberately uses taught 'email' to keep the remainder minimal.

exercises.prompt: first name · last name · email address · form · Mr · Ms
exercises.rationale: Form field labels are sight vocabulary: learners must recognize them instantly on paper and screens before any completion task.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Match the spoken question to the form field.]
exercises.rationale: Intake interviews are spoken forms: mapping each known question onto its written field label is the transfer this lesson exists for.

exercises.prompt: [L1: What kind of information is each of these? Match it to the field.]
exercises.rationale: Recognizing value formats (@ and dot = email, digit groups = phone) lets learners orient on a real form even when they cannot read every label.

exercises.prompt:
Form
First name — Sara
Last name — Diaz
Country — Brazil
Phone number — 555-0192

She is from ___. Her ___ name is Diaz.
exercises.rationale: Reading a filled form and extracting facts from it; the first/last distractor pair targets the field-label confusion es speakers carry from nombre/apellido order differences.

exercises.prompt: [L1: Put the words in order to ask for the missing field.]
exercises.rationale: Learners completing a form for someone else must ask this; extends the L10 WH-frame with the new field vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 0.75x] 'Hello, I'm Sara Diaz, your teacher.' — [L1: What do you call her?]
exercises.rationale: Band §4 pragmatics note for Mr/Ms verbatim: titles go with the LAST name; this is a high-frequency politeness error in school and intake settings.

options.label: Ms Diaz.
options.rationale: Title + last name: Ms works for any adult woman, married or not.

options.label: Ms Sara.
options.rationale: Title + first name — the most common ESL transfer (common politeness pattern in es/ar/vi contexts, but not standard English).

options.label: Teacher Sara.
options.rationale: Occupation used as a title — direct transfer from classroom cultures where 'Teacher' is a form of address.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 1.0x] 'I speak English.' — [L1: Which is the correct WRITTEN form of what you hear?]
exercises.rationale: Capitalization of proper nouns is in the §2 objective; Spanish writes language names lowercase (inglés), so the lowercase-language error is the targeted transfer.

options.label: I speak English.
options.rationale: Language names are proper nouns in English and always take a capital letter.

options.label: I speak english.
options.rationale: Direct es transfer: Spanish writes languages lowercase (inglés, español) — English never does.

options.label: i speak English.
options.rationale: Catches losing the sentence-start capital (and lowercase i), the other capitalization rule forms are graded on.

exercises.prompt: [audio, 2 plays: 0.75x then 1.0x] 'My last name is Diaz.'
exercises.scoring: case-sensitive on Diaz: the capital D is the graded point; rest case-insensitive
exercises.rationale: Writing a heard proper noun with its capital letter — exactly what happens when an official spells a name at a counter and the learner fills the form.

exercises.prompt: [audio] 'What's your last name?' → [L1: Answer with your real last name, in a full sentence.]
asr_focus: full frame produced, not the bare name alone
first/last not swapped (checked against profile if available)
exercises.rationale: Intake officials ask exactly this; answering with the frame instead of a bare name keeps the exchange self-correcting when fields get confused.

exercises.prompt: [L1: WRITTEN chat. The AI is a school receptionist completing a form for you. It asks your first name, last name, country, phone number and email address, one by one. Type each answer.]
exercises.rationale: End-to-end rehearsal of the form-completion scenario in the written mode the §2 tag (P-written) requires; typing forces the capitalization rules ex7/ex8 taught.
